description.narrative:
A state-wide tripartite strategy on sustainable development of natural stone industry was conceptualised and adopted by the State Government of Rajasthan. The integrated strategy has a major focus on occupational safety and health (OSH) and links to State silicosis policy, besides gender, fundamental principles and right at work (FPRW), wages and others. The state level strategy has strong resonance with the "Industry Policy" that Global call to action for a human-centred recovery from the COVID-19 crisis highlights, and aims to promote Rajasthan as a responsible sourcing state and destination for investment in the stone sector by paving the way for formalisation of the sector, dominated by informal and road side worksheds in peri-urban and rural settings. State Labour Department of Rajasthan developed an OSH flipbook for the stone sector for raising awareness on good practices among employers and workers, as a step towards reaching informal workplaces located in peri-urban and rural areas in the lower tier of supply chain of stone industry. A comprehensive ILO report "Challenges and Opportunities For Productive Employment and Decent Work in the Natural Stone Mining Industry Supply Chain in Rajasthan" based on desk review and primary survey, has facilitated systematic understanding among key stakeholders about the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats for the sector, including in relation to international market trends. Building on the study findings, a draft tripartite state-wide strategy for the sustainable development of the sector has been developed in consultation with constituents and under leadership of the Department of Industry, State Government of Rajasthan.
To improve OSH awareness and practises in the stone sector, the ILO supported the development of an OSH visual flipbook, in consultation with State government for dissemination and capacity building targeting informal economic units and workers dominating the sector.
The ILO organized a stakeholder dialogue between Rajasthan and buyers/ constituents and investors from Europe for the State Government of Rajasthan to unveil the tripartite state-wide strategy.

description.narrative:
As part of the implementation of the Wage Code adopted in 2019, the Ministry of Labour and Employment (MoLE) published in July 2020, the draft rules of the Code on Wages, which define how the national floor-level minimum wage will be operationalized. In addition, in March 2021, the rules concerning the functioning of the Central Advisory Board (CAB), which handles issues related to minimum wages, were notified.
The draft rules were finalized in late 2021.
These reforms will bring new dynamics to the minimum wage system in India, as the States will have to fix their respective minimum rates of wages at least equal to or above the floor wage. The effect could raise the wage levels of up to 74 million low-paid workers, either presently not covered under the minimum wage regulation or receiving a sub-minimum level of wages.
The new floors will benefit particularly women, overrepresented at the low end of the wage distribution, reducing one of the highest gender pay gaps in the region.
The draft rules introduced criteria for the wage setting procedure encouraging the use of evidence-based information. Consequently, social partners have an unprecedented opportunity to use evidence and social dialogue to determine adequate minimum wages.
Finally, the Code on Wages has done away with fixing occupational minimum wage rates or wage fixation by scheduled employments. It has only retained minimum wages by skill categories or geographical areas, or both. The change reduces the number of rates to a minimum of 4 and a maximum of 12 rates per state. The simplification aims to facilitate implementing an adequate minimum wage policy and enhancing compliance. The ILO has a longstanding collaboration with the Ministry of Labour and Employment (MoLE) and social partners on the subject of adequate minimum wages in India. ILO technical inputs to the draft rules of the Code on Wages were provided through the Economic Survey 2018-19, which is a programmatic document of the Ministry of Finance guiding the policy agenda in India. A whole chapter was devoted to the issue of redesigning a Minimum Wage System to promote Inclusive Growth. The draft rules of the Code of Wages, published in July 2020, are a close reflection of the recommendations provided by the Ministry of Finance with close ILO technical advice in the Economic Survey. Once the draft rules were published, MoLE called for public feedback for 45 days from July 7, 2020. In support of this process, the ILO produced and shared a policy discussion paper addressing both benefits and shortcomings of the Code of Wages rules. It drew attention to the shortcomings in terms of coverage and the criteria for setting the minimum wage, linking it to other developments such as the methodology used by the Expert Committee Report 2019 – on which the ILO also previously provided technical advice, with support from a TC project (GLO 1823/NL) funded by the Netherlands. Two workshops on the ILO policy discussion paper and the draft Code of Wages were held with Workers Organisations (the Workers Charters and all of India's 12 Trade Unions) in August 2020. In addition, the joint analysis of ILO and V.V. Giri (the national labour institute attached to the Ministry of Labour and Employment) was made public and disseminated in February 2021 through publication in the Indian Journal called Economic & Political Weekly, which addressed the Code on Wages and rules' implications on effective minimum wage policy. The machinery of minimum wage fixing, including the role of Central Advisory Boards, was the subject of training activities and workshops with ViviGiri in 2019 and earlier.
